summary: KERNEL CONTEST: The codified European Central Bank mandate (the shared text) read strictly as requiring only price stability (the orthodox reading) versus read expansively to include secondary objectives like climate transition and employment. Each reading alters the beneficiaries and scope of monetary intervention[cite: 2, 3].

KERNEL CONTEST: The constitutional war powers allocation (the fixed legal kernel) read as requiring explicit legislative authorization (congressional primacy reading) versus read as granting inherent, unilateral defense authority to the executive branch. The contest determines the structural limits of state coercion and who holds the legitimate authority to adjudicate it[cite: 2].

KERNEL CONTEST: The EU's foundational voting rule for foreign policy (the shared institutional kernel) read as an essential guarantor of member-state sovereignty (preventing forced coordination) versus read as a structural veto-trap that enables minoritarian extraction. Competing readings of the exact same rule yield entirely different structural constraints[cite: 2, 3].

KERNEL CONTEST: The corpus of common law precedent (a practice-based kernel) read via strict stare decisis as a binding, backward-looking constraint versus read as a dynamic, evolutionary framework adaptable to contemporary norms. An authority-grounding contest where practice itself is the contested substrate[cite: 2].

KERNEL CONTEST: The definition of 'legitimate knowledge' (an implicit or practice-based kernel) read via credentialed institutional expertise (a centralized, methodological reading) versus distributed, experiential, or pluralistic validation. The contest dictates who has the authority to participate in the epistemic commons[cite: 2].
